meta.title: Who really said "No Respect for a Man Who Can Spell a Word Only One Way"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Andrew Jackson. It is the punch line of an 1855 newspaper anecdote; Jackson died in 1845 and was first credited with it in 1882.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'No Respect for a Man Who Can Spell a Word Only One Way'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Andrew Jackson. The line began as an 1855 courtroom joke, went to Mark Twain in 1875, and reached Jackson only in 1882.

answer.label: Not Andrew Jackson — an anonymous 1855 newspaper joke
answer.authorDates: American newspaper humor · first printed 31 August 1855
answer.sourceLine: The line is the punch line of a comic courtroom anecdote about an unlettered country lawyer, printed in the Jamestown Journal of 31 August 1855 and reprinted that November in Harper’s New Monthly Magazine. Mark Twain was credited with it in 1875 and Andrew Jackson not until 1882 — thirty-seven years after Jackson’s death — and no source in Jackson’s own words has ever been found.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Jamestown Journal (Jamestown, New York), 31 August 1855, p. 3
Harper’s New Monthly Magazine, “Editor’s Drawer,” November 1855, p. 860
July 1882 — thirty-seven years after his death

source.excerpt: Some years ago the Hon. Hiram Runnels, of Wyoming, Pennsylvania, had quite a reputation as a pettifogger. His knowledge of books was very small, and his main reliance was upon his own tact and shrewdness, which rarely failed him, and lasts to this day. On one occasion he was pitted against a smart, well-dressed limb of the law from the city, who made fun of a paper which Runnels had submitted to the court. … Runnels replied: “The learned counsel on the other side finds fault with my spellin’, as though the merits of the case depended on sich outside matters. I’m agin luggin’ in any sich forin’ affairs, but I will say that a man must be a great fool who can’t spell a word more than one way.”
trail: 31 August 1855 — the earliest instance located by Quote Investigator ↗: an anecdote in the Jamestown Journal in which the pettifogger Hon. Nyrum Reynolds of Wyoming County tells a jury that “a man must be a d—d fool, who can’t spell a word more than one way.”

November 1855 — the same story runs in the “Editor’s Drawer” of Harper’s New Monthly Magazine, p. 860 ↗, with the lawyer renamed Hon. Hiram Runnels of Wyoming, Pennsylvania, and the oath softened to “a great fool.”

November 1875 — the Illinois Schoolmaster, p. 380 ↗ opens an essay on spelling drill with “Mark Twain says that he must have little genius who can’t spell a word in more than one way” — the first famous name attached to the joke.
July 1882 — the New England Historical and Genealogical Register, p. 273 ↗ invokes “General Jackson” for the sentiment, the earliest Jackson connection on record.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the scanned volume at the Internet Archive; the dialect spelling is the magazine’s own. In the earlier Jamestown Journal version, the lawyer is Hon. Nyrum Reynolds of Wyoming County, New York, and the oath is uncensored: “a man must be a d—d fool, who can’t spell a word more than one way.”

source.rightsNote: The 1855 anecdote excerpted above is comfortably in the public domain in the United States — Harper’s New Monthly Magazine for November 1855 is long out of copyright, as is the 1882 Register. The one-line modern wording credited to Andrew Jackson, however, has never been tied to any datable work of his or anyone else’s, so we assert no rights status for it.

author.name: Andrew Jackson
author.heading: The man the joke got pinned on
author.bio: Andrew Jackson was born in the Waxhaw settlement on the Carolina border on 15 March 1767, rose to fame as a general, served in both houses of Congress, and was president from 1829 to 1837; he died at the Hermitage near Nashville on 8 June 1845. He was relentlessly lampooned by his opponents as an unlettered frontiersman, and, as Ralph Keyes notes in The Quote Verifier, “particularly ridiculed for being a poor speller” — which is precisely why a ready-made joke about creative spelling drifted onto him decades after he was gone. The same reputation attracted other inventions, including the mangled order “Elevate them guns a little lower.”

Attribution history traced in Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: No Respect for a Man Who Can Spell a Word Only One Way,” 25 June 2010, updated 28 January 2025.

misattribution.heading: Everyone it has been pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is a floating gag, and it has been handed to a new famous name roughly every generation. None of the claimants has a source.

items.why: The earliest Jackson link Quote Investigator located is an aside in the New England Historical and Genealogical Register for July 1882 ↗, p. 273: town clerks spelled their office so many ways that “evidently, like General Jackson, they despised a man who could spell a word in only one way.” Jackson had died in 1845, thirty-seven years earlier, and even this instance is a passing simile rather than a quotation of him.

Quote Investigator reports that the saying “has never been found in the writings or speeches of Mark Twain,” yet the November 1875 Illinois Schoolmaster ↗ opens an editorial on spelling with “Mark Twain says that he must have little genius who can’t spell a word in more than one way.” Twain was alive and famous at the time and never appears to have claimed it.

Monticello’s Thomas Jefferson Encyclopedia files the line as a spurious quotation ↗, giving 1983 as the earliest appearance credited to Jefferson — in Peter McWilliams’s The Word Processing Book, p. 57. Jefferson in fact told his daughter in 1783 to “take care that you never spell a word wrong.”

items.who: G. K. Chesterton and W. C. Fields
items.why: Both appear on Monticello’s list of other attributions ↗ for the same saying, alongside Jackson and Twain, with no source offered for either.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the remark “was created as the punch line of a fictional anecdote about spelling” and was only later reassigned to famous figures — and that the evidence for Twain or Jackson is very weak.

context.heading: A joke that needed a famous mouth
lead: The remark was born as the tag line of a story, not as anyone’s opinion. In the 1855 telling a rustic but shrewd country lawyer is mocked in open court for his spelling, and wins the jury by shrugging the objection off — the humour depends on the speaker being a bit of a fool, which is exactly the flavour that later got lost when the line was handed to a president.

That handover follows a pattern quotle.info sees constantly: an unowned joke drifts toward whichever famous name makes it funniest. Mark Twain got it first, in an 1875 schoolteachers’ journal ↗, because he really did write that he never had “any large respect for good spelling.” Jackson got it later because his enemies had spent decades painting him as a man who could barely spell his own name.
context.detailsSummary: The Harvard story, and the other version you have seen
detailsBody: The wording most often pinned on Jackson is not the one in this page’s title but “It is a damn poor mind indeed which can’t think of at least two ways to spell any word.” Wikiquote lists that sentence under “Attributed to Andrew Jackson” ↗, flags it as likely misattributed with a link to Quote Investigator, and says it is only sometimes reported as a retort to John Quincy Adams, who boycotted Harvard’s 1833 award of an honorary doctorate to Jackson. Wikiquote traces that framing to a 1987 journalism textbook, M. Mencher’s News Reporting and Writing, 4th edition — not to any contemporary record.

The same entry records “Never trust a man who has only one way to spell a word” as an unsourced variant. Variant-hopping like this is itself a warning sign: a real quotation tends to have one stable wording tied to one document, while a floating gag reshapes itself every time it is retold.
context.pull: Quote Investigator: “the supporting evidence for an ascription to Twain or Jackson is very weak.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's article "Quote Origin: No Respect for a Man Who Can Spell a Word Only One Way" (posted 25 June 2010, updated 28 January 2025) states the saying has never been found in Twain's writings or speeches, gives the earliest instance as an anecdote about Hon. Nyrum Reynolds in the Jamestown Journal of 31 August 1855, the November 1855 Harper's retelling with Hiram Runnels, the 1875 Illinois Schoolmaster Twain credit, and an 1882 New England Historical and Genealogical Register Jackson instance; it concludes the remark was created as the punch line of a fictional anecdote and that "the supporting evidence for an ascription to Twain or Jackson is very weak," noting Jackson died in 1845 and all located citations postdate his death.

The scanned full text of Harper's New Monthly Magazine Vol. XI contains, on p. 860, the Editor's Drawer anecdote of Hon. Hiram Runnels of Wyoming, Pennsylvania, ending "a man must be a great fool who can't spell a word more than one way."
The Internet Archive item page for Harper's New Monthly Magazine Volume 11, June to November 1855, exists and hosts the scanned volume.

The scanned full text of The Illinois Schoolmaster vol. 8 contains, on p. 380 under the heading SPELLING, the sentence "Mark Twain says that he must have little genius who can't spell a word in more than one way."
The Internet Archive item page for The Illinois Schoolmaster (the volume containing the November 1875 issue) exists and hosts the scanned volume.

The scanned full text of the New England Historical and Genealogical Register, July 1882, Vol. 36, contains on p. 273: "The variety of ways in which Groton Town-Clerks contrived to spell the same office is marvellous to behold. Evidently, like General Jackson, they despised a man who could spell a word in only one way."
The Internet Archive item page for the New England Historical and Genealogical Register, 1882-07, Vol. 36, exists and hosts the scanned issue.

Wikiquote's Andrew Jackson page lists "It is a damn poor mind indeed which can't think of at least two ways to spell any word" under the section "Attributed to Andrew Jackson," notes it is sometimes reported as a retort to John Quincy Adams over Harvard's 1833 honorary degree (citing M. Mencher, News Reporting and Writing, 4th ed., 1987), records the unsourced variant "Never trust a man who has only one way to spell a word," and links Quote Investigator with the label "Likely misattributed."

Monticello's Thomas Jefferson Encyclopedia entry "Spell a word only one way (Spurious Quotation)" gives the quotation as "I have nothing but contempt for anyone who can spell a word only one way," lists other attributions as Andrew Jackson, Mark Twain, G.K. Chesterton and W.C. Fields, dates the earliest known appearance in print to 1880 (per the Yale Book of Quotations) and the earliest Jefferson credit to 1983 (Peter McWilliams, The Word Processing Book, p. 57), quotes Jefferson's 1783 letter to his daughter "Take care that you never spell a word wrong," and cites Ralph Keyes's conclusion that it is simply an "old gag."

Wikipedia's Andrew Jackson article gives his birth date as 15 March 1767 in the Waxhaw Settlement, his death as 8 June 1845 in Nashville, Tennessee, and his presidency as the seventh, from 4 March 1829 to 4 March 1837.
